newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Stranded China dissidents fearful as HK '97 nears.
newsitem.headline: Stranded China dissidents fearful as HK '97 nears.

text.p: A dozen Chinese dissidents are still stranded in Hong Kong and fear British colonial rulers are too busy preparing their own pullout to worry about resettling them before Communist China takes over on July 1.

The dissidents, who have sneaked into Hong Kong in recent years, are afraid the post-handover administration will send them back to China because they do not have right of abode in the territory, a human rights activist said on Tuesday.

"They are very frightened because they are afraid they cannot remain after July 1 and will be sent back to China," Frank Lu, a spokesman for the Information Centre of Human Rights and Democratic Movement in China, told Reuters.
Fearful of China's political clout after it takes back Hong Kong, a British colony for 156 years, scores of mainland dissidents have fled abroad in recent months, Lu said.

Six left for Sweden last week, amongst them Shao Jiang, one of the student activists who took part in the 1989 pro-democracy movement in Beijing which ended in the bloody military crackdown in Tiananmen Square.
Lu said the British-led administration, which had helped dozens of dissidents find sanctuary in the run-up to the handover, was now too preoccupied with its own departure.
"Now the British government here is not really helping because they are also packing up to go," Lu said.
The British-led government said it did not comment on such matters.

Lu said the dissidents' fear was real, noting that Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa had unveiled a bill tightening residency rights after July 1. Tung was picked by Beijing to run the territory after the handover.
Tung has said people who entered illegally will not be allowed to stay automatically after the handover and must get approval from the immigration chief.
Lu, who holds no permanent right of abode, plans to remain after the handover but fears this new requirement in the future may be a way to squeeze him out -- and back to China.
"I worry I may not get permanent residency because after July 1, I must get approval from the immigration director," Lu said.
Lu was jailed for a year for his involvement in the 1989 pro-democracy movement in China and managed to escape to Hong Kong during another prison term in Hunan province in 1993.
